issues.legal_issue: A court exercising writ jurisdiction may not impose general directions that legislate or conflict with governing allotment rules, but may issue case-related directions and clarifications consistent with those rules.
material_facts: The government had notified allotment rules that had been approved by the Supreme Court and amended over time.
A Single Judge, while hearing an individual allotment dispute, issued general directions governing several aspects of government-house allotments.
The Administration appealed, arguing that the directions conflicted with the governing rules.
issues.conclusion: The Single Judge could not impose directions that conflicted with the allotment rules or amounted to legislation. Directions that merely clarified the rules and were consistent with them could be retained; other directions were set aside or modified.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 32 and 226 empower courts to issue appropriate directions, but a High Court does not exercise a power akin to Article 142 and cannot rewrite rules or act as an appellate authority over administrative decisions. Courts may address gaps or exceptional circumstances with caution, and directions must not conflict with laws in force or Supreme Court directions. The Court relied on Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, Union of India v. M. Bhaskar, E.S.P. Rajaram v. Union of India, Guruvayoor Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan, Reliance Airport Developers (P) Ltd. v. Airport Authority of India, Chandigarh Administration v. Manpreet Singh, and P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka, as well as the earlier Supreme Court decision approving the draft allotment rules.

predicates.appeal_challenges_general_allotment_dire: An appeal challenges general judicial directions made in a dispute about government accommodation allotments.
predicates.governing_rules_exist: Rules governing the relevant government accommodation allotments are in force.
predicates.directions_conflict_with_rules: The challenged directions conflict with the governing rules or impose a general scheme that is legislative in nature.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges general allotment directions, rules govern the subject, and the directions conflict with those rules or legislate generally, the conflicting directions are set aside or modified.

issues.legal_issue: A new house should not be earmarked for a category or post while the previously earmarked house for that category or post remains occupied and has not returned to the general pool.
material_facts: The allotment rules provided for earmarking houses for specified officers or categories and for placing unearmarked houses in the general pool.
An existing earmarked house could remain occupied by an officer who was no longer entitled to that accommodation.
The Single Judge directed that another house should not be earmarked for the same category or post until the occupied house was vacated, subject to an identified exception.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the clarification, with the stated exception, and directed that a new house for a category or post not be earmarked until the existing earmarked house had been vacated and placed in the general pool.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 7 provides for earmarking houses and a general pool. The Court considered the clarification consistent with the rule's purpose and directed that only one house be earmarked for a category or post as needed, subject to the exception already made for the specified post. The Court relied on the Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration General Pool) Allotment Rules, 1996, particularly Rule 7.

predicates.government_accommodation_allotment_proce: The matter concerns the allotment and earmarking of government accommodation.
predicates.a_house_is_earmarked_for_a_category_or_p: An existing house has been set aside for a specified category or post.
predicates.the_existing_earmarked_house_remains_occ: The house already set aside for that category or post remains occupied and has not been returned to the general pool.

issues.definition: If an allotment proceeding concerns an earmarked house that remains occupied, no additional house is earmarked for that category or post until the occupied house is vacated and returned to the general pool.

issues.legal_issue: Out-of-turn allotments and the exercise of coordination and control powers must be constrained by committee recommendations, recorded reasons and supporting material, and an overall annual limit; allotments based on the undefined functional-requirements ground are impermissible.
material_facts: The allotment rules allowed specified out-of-turn allotments and identified an authority with coordination and control powers over housing pools.
The rules and guidelines did not explain the expression functional requirements or provide guidance for its application.
The rules imposed a ten-percent limit on out-of-turn allotments, while the Single Judge had imposed an absolute prohibition on out-of-turn allotments and discretionary allotments.
The Court found that the authority's coordination power did not itself authorize discretionary allotments outside the substantive rules.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected an absolute ban on out-of-turn allotments, but directed that the relevant powers be exercised only on the House Allotment Committee's recommendation, supported by reasons related to job requirements and supporting data; no allotment could be made under the functional-requirements ground, and out-of-turn allotments could not exceed ten percent of all houses allotted in a year. The coordination and control power could not be used as an independent discretionary allotment power.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 8 and 11 govern coordination and control and out-of-turn allotments. Rule 11 is comprehensive as to permissible out-of-turn situations, but its functional-requirements ground is vague and unguided. The ten-percent limit applies to the entire exercise under Rules 8 and 11. Discretion must be exercised fairly, for relevant purposes, and with reasons and supporting material. The Court relied on the Allotment Rules, including Rules 8 and 11, and the related guidelines.

predicates.an_authority_proposes_an_out_of_turn_or_: An authority proposes to use out-of-turn allotment powers or coordination and control powers in making an allotment.

issues.definition: When an authority proposes an out-of-turn or coordinated allotment in a government accommodation matter, the allotment must be recommended by the committee, supported by reasons and data, stay within the annual limit, and not rely on undefined functional requirements.

issues.legal_issue: The rules do not require advance publication of prospective allotments or an objection process, but the final list of allotments must be published online.
material_facts: The allotment rules required applications and provided for allotment by category and seniority, including a safeguard for maintaining the seniority list.
The rules did not require publication of a prospective-allottees list or invitations for objections before allotment.
The Single Judge had ordered advance publication and objections; the Court considered that process unnecessary and likely to delay allotments.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the requirements to publish a prospective-allottees list and invite objections, but directed that the final list of allotments made by the House Allotment Committee be placed on the government website.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 9 sets out the application and allotment process, including category-wise seniority, and Rule 9(5) safeguards the seniority list. In the absence of a rule requiring objections to proposed allotments, courts should not impose an additional process that would delay and complicate administration. The Court relied on Rules 9 and 9(5) of the Allotment Rules.

predicates.government_accommodation_allotment_proce: The matter concerns the allotment of government accommodation.
predicates.the_rules_provide_for_applications_and_s: The governing rules set out an application and seniority process but do not require objections to a prospective-allottees list.

issues.definition: Where allotment rules provide for applications and seniority but not objections to proposed allotments, advance objections are unnecessary, while the final allotment list must be published online.

issues.legal_issue: A government servant should not ordinarily receive two separate government houses, and any exception allowing multiple houses must be invoked sparingly on the allotment committee's recommendation.
material_facts: The Court was informed that some government servants or their families were being allotted one house in Chandigarh and another elsewhere in the same state.
No general rule authorizing two such houses was identified, although the rules contemplated a limited circumstance in which two houses could be allotted.
The Court noted that the multiple-house provision should be used only in exceptional circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The State was directed not to allot two different houses to one government servant, subject to the limited circumstances recognized by the rules; that exception must be invoked sparingly and only upon the House Allotment Committee's recommendation.
issues.legal_principle: In the absence of a general rule authorizing two houses, the State should not allot two different houses to one government servant. Rule 11(1)(b) permits an exceptional situation, but it is to be invoked sparingly and on the House Allotment Committee's recommendation. The Court relied on Rule 11(1)(b) of the Allotment Rules.

predicates.government_accommodation_allotment_proce: The matter concerns government accommodation allotments.
predicates.a_government_servant_is_proposed_to_rece: The State proposes to allot two separate government houses to the same government servant.

issues.definition: If the State proposes to give one government servant two houses, the allotment is barred unless exceptional circumstances justify it and the committee recommends it.

issues.legal_issue: A discretionary extension allowing a government servant to retain accommodation beyond the prescribed retention period is invalid when it lacks guiding criteria and operates against the interests of employees awaiting accommodation.
material_facts: The allotment rules specified retention periods for different circumstances and allowed a further extension in exceptional cases on payment of a higher licence fee.
The rules did not define exceptional cases or provide guidelines for deciding whether an extension should be granted.
Employees awaiting allotments were deprived of accommodation while others retained houses beyond the specified periods.
The Court found the prescribed charge minimal compared with market rent.
issues.conclusion: The Court held the discretionary extension provision unsustainable and directed that no authority entertain a claim to retain government accommodation beyond the specified retention periods.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 13(1) and 13(2) provide specific retention periods and reasonable time to vacate; Rule 13(5) permitted extensions in exceptional cases but contained no guiding criteria. Unguided discretion that allows continued occupation and disadvantages employees awaiting accommodation is arbitrary. The Court relied on Rule 13(1), Rule 13(2), and Rule 13(5) of the Allotment Rules.

predicates.government_accommodation_retention_proce: The matter concerns a government servant's retention of allotted government accommodation.
predicates.the_rules_set_retention_periods: The governing rules specify periods within which a government servant must vacate the accommodation.
predicates.an_extension_power_has_no_guiding_criter: The rules permit an extension beyond those periods but do not state criteria to guide the decision.

issues.definition: When rules set retention periods but an extension power has no guiding criteria, retention beyond the prescribed period is not permitted.

issues.legal_issue: An officer who must vacate an occupied earmarked house but is entitled to government accommodation in another category must be provided an alternative accommodation, with suitable private accommodation as a fallback if government accommodation is unavailable.
material_facts: The appellant occupied an earmarked house and claimed entitlement to accommodation corresponding to her appointment as a State Information Commissioner.
The dispute about eviction and damages remained pending before the High Court.
The Supreme Court directed the State to provide accommodation in the category corresponding to her appointment and required her to vacate the house she occupied after the alternative was provided.
The Court specified a fallback if accommodation in her category was unavailable.
issues.conclusion: The State was directed to provide the appellant an alternative accommodation in the category to which she was entitled, and she was to vacate her existing house after that allotment. If accommodation in her category was unavailable, the State had to provide appropriate accommodation, including private accommodation of her status.
issues.legal_principle: The Court made a case-specific interim direction without deciding the pending eviction and damages dispute, leaving those issues to the High Court. The direction required accommodation corresponding to the officer's entitlement, with appropriate accommodation as a fallback if the relevant government accommodation was unavailable.

predicates.government_accommodation_appeal_involves: An appeal concerning government accommodation involves a person who occupies a government house.
predicates.the_occupant_is_entitled_to_an_alternati: The occupant is entitled to accommodation in a category different from the house currently occupied.
predicates.that_alternative_is_to_be_provided: The authority is directed to provide the occupant with accommodation corresponding to that entitlement.

issues.definition: If an occupant in a government accommodation appeal is entitled to another category and that alternative is to be provided, the authority must provide it, the occupant must then vacate the existing house, and suitable private accommodation must be supplied if necessary.
